tweets: Peptides are injected because most can't survive digestion. Here's why pills don't work (yet) for most peptides, and what SNAC tech changes:
Your stomach is a peptide shredder. Digestive enzymes break peptide bonds—the same bonds holding therapeutic peptides together. Oral bioavailability is often <1%. That's why injections dominate.

SNAC (sodium N-[8-(2-hydroxybenzoyl)amino]caprylate) is a carrier that temporarily shields peptides from digestion. It's how oral semaglutide works. But it's not magic—bioavailability is still single-digit % vs injections.

Pills have obvious appeal, but current tech means: lower efficacy (fraction of dose absorbed), higher cost (more peptide wasted), and less predictable dosing than injections. Tradeoffs matter in clinical use.
